speechtext: (Translation.) Many are called but few are chosen.

subtopic: ALBERT DECARY, CHARLES J. BAILLAIRGEON, N.P.
speechtext:
(Translation.) I am in earnest when I say that the Liberal party will soon get into power. What will the Liberals have to do? They will have to attend to the construction of the Georgian Bay canal. The boards of trade, the great corporations, the higher branches of commerce, the railway companies are clamoring for it. I am for the construction of the Georgian Bay canal, which is a necessary undertaking asked for by every administration, whether conservative or liberal. The Government has so far made enormous sacrifices in order to lay out the route, to have soundings taken so as to know what was the obstruction in the way, what would be the probable cost; in short, to ascertain whether that route would be advantageous to the country.
What did they find? They found that the Northern route would cost about $110,000,000, while the Southern route would entail an expenditure of only $95,000,000. It might be a little more to-day. The figures I have given out might not be the exact amount, but we shall take it as the approximate cost of the building of the canal.
The canal would shorten considerably the distance from Georgian Bay to London; some say it would make it about 400 miles shorter, which means a saving of from

$100,000,000 to $150,000,000. If the money were spent carefully, it would be of a great benefit to the country, for it would keep at least 15,000 people at work during ten years. Is it not worth undertaking the building of that canal and should we not consider carefully the advisability of starting the work? The Chambre de Commerce and the Board of Trade of Montreal, the largest companies, the banks and the leading financial firms of the country are crying out for the construction of the Georgian Bay Canal.
I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that hon. gentlemen are not much concerned with the interest of the people since they do not listen to the advice of our leading citizens. We must build that canal. I was anxious to visit Georgian Bay; I went there and I saw the place. I realize that it would be a great mistake, -and even more, to postpone any longer the building of the canal. Connecting Georgian Bay with lake Nipissing, there is Trent river, then Turtle river, the Mattawa and Ottawa rivers to the island of Montreal, and then you may go right through to Europe without transhipment, and reduce the cost of transportation by about one or two cents for every bushel of wheat. Then why should we not build that canal instead of spending millions as we are doing now? The liberal party which will be called to replace the present government will undertake it. Hon. gentlemen may say:
Why did you not undertake the construction of the canal during the fifteen years you remained in power? The answer is very simple: the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier had undertaken considerable works, such as the Quebec Bridge, the Hudson Bay Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific; he wanted to have them completed before starting on the Georgian Bay Canal. That is what I would answer to hon. gentlemen. Instead of spending our money here and there without any necessity and without any advantage to the country, they should have undertaken that work. I say that the present government is not worthy of the confidence of the people and should not remain in office any longer. Before long we shall have to build the canal.
There is another thing to ido and I have asked for it many times: I am referring to the building of a bridge between Vaudreuil and Ste. Anne. I have asked the government for assistance in order that we may build that bridge. What did they answer? They said they had no money. No money for bridges at Ste. Anne and Vaudreuil; they

are in the province of Quebec, they are not international bridges and there are no funds available for works of that kind. Did the millions spent in Vancouver apply to an international undertaking? And what about the money given to St. John and Halifax? They gave us that answer like a man who does not wish to answer at all. When you do not wish to help you always have a good answer to give. But I say that it is a shame to delay the construction of Vaudreuil-St. Anne bridge any longer. Think of an important city like Montreal, with a population of 600,000, whose people to pass from the island, have to use canoes, and the same lack of facilities is felt as regards vehicles.
People have been drowned, lives have been lost, because of this condition of things. And when we ask the hon. ministers who represent the Province of Quebec to help us in building the bridges, we are told: "It cannot be done, sir, there is no money, The time will come when you will discover that the people are getting restless; the hon. mambers will realize that the people are irritated, that they are getting angry; the time will come when hon. gentlemen will have to account for their doings, and the more grasping will have been the administration, the more severe will we be with these gentlemen.
What is the next plank of our platform? We have already stated what the liberals will do: We shall exact an account from those who govern us. We shalll ask for an account of the millions which they have had in hand since 1911. We shall enquire what has become of those millions. Where are those millions which have been given you in the people's interest? We shall have a great, national investigation, there will be no cuts and thrusts, but we will investigate everywhere, we will make a thorough search of all the public departements, asking the hon. gentlemen to produce vouchers for the money which has been entrusted to them. Then will they find the time long, then will they find that the people are severe, then will they find it difficult to produce an account with vouchers. Yet, that is what we shall ask them to do. We shall ask them how it happens that public offices are filled with employees of all nationalities, except French-Cana-dians. We will demand from those who represent the Province of Quebec the reason why they have tolerated such discrimination. You have but to visit the Publics Works and all the large departments, and take a list of those who are there, to realize
how unfairly our compatriots have been treated. The liberal party will see that all be reinstated who have been dismissed, turned out, without an investigation being made, or with but a semblance of investigation, and this, because their only sin, their only fault, was that they were liberals. Our friends who have been turned out of power will be returned to their respective positions. We shall investigate and find out why these gentlemen have been driven out of power. We shall have no difficulty,
I assure you, in proving the flagrant injustice which has beeen done them.
It is said, Mr. Speaker, that Quebec is isolated. My hon. friends on the other side of the House will forgive me, but, the Province of Quebec is not isolated. Have we not three ministers in the Cabinet? Have we not the hon. minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) who represents the Catholics, those who speak French as well as those who speak English? Is he not an honourable man? Does he not represent us in the Cabinet? Have we not the hon. minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne) in the Cabinet? Have we not the hon. Mr. Blondin in the Senate? It is true that he was beaten twice, but he has been given a seat in the Senate as a compensation for these two defeats: "Go, take a seat in the Senate, sir, you will be given a portfolio, you shall represent the Montreal electors". We have three ministers in the Cabinet. We are told that Quebec is isolated? Not at all, though we may not have all that should be coming to us, notwithstanding our three representatives. They are honourable, distinguished men, who represent us as well as they can.
There is another thing which astonishes me, Mr. Speaker, that is, that, the liberal unionists should have such little influence in the Union Cabinet which is formed of liberal and conservative unionists. Have not four judges been appointed lately? Is there a "rouge-bleu" amongst them? Is there a liberal judge amongst the four who have been apointed? Where then are the unionists? What influence have these gentlemen that they should have been silent in the face of those appointments? What is the influence of the Liberal-Unionists, of the so-called Liberals who are Conservatives? What is the influence of these gentlemen? I would have thought that the unionist ministers would have had something to do with the Government, but, judging from evidence, they are doing absolutely nothing, they let everything go, swallow every new appointment, without a protest.

We are not isolated, but we are badly represented.
They shall have to face those from whom they have withdrawn the right to vote: the people who had comme to settle in this country at the cost of great sacrifices; they who have been disfranchised for fear that they would vote against the Government. That is an injustice.
They will get a square deal at the hands of the Liberals who will be called upon to form a government in place of this unfortunate administration; they will be given back their franchise of which - I shall not use too harsh a word because I might be called to order by the chair - they were so unscrupulously deprived.

subtopic: ALBERT DECARY, CHARLES J. BAILLAIRGEON, N.P.
speechtext:
(Translation.) I
dislike to so characterize it, but that is the actual fact.
I remember a contest which gave me much trouble; I had to work day and night. It was the election in Chateauguay and Hon. Sydney Fisher was the candidate. The distinguished and elderly gentleman had accepted to contest the seat in Chateauguay. His opponent was Mr. Morris who, along with his good conservative friends of Ottawa, had caused the people to believe that a bridge would be built from Chateauguay towards Lachine as well as a dam at Caughnawaga. Vainly did we keep telling them that it was merely an electoral scheme, that there was no sincerity in such promises, that it was a subterfuge and they should not rely on such promises. Hon. Mr. Sevigny was there, going through the country and promising the construction of the Chateauguay bridge, and so the people of Beauharnois, Chateauguay and Huntingdon actually believed that a bridge would be built. In vain did we assure them: " It is all nonsense, you know very well that the government will not build that bridge ". They replied: " We are sure to get our bridge ". Well, it turned out that the bridge never was built and the thing was not even mentioned after the election. I say to hon. gentlemen opposite: Before Hon. Mr. Fisher leaves this world, will you be gentlemanly enough to go and apologize to him? Will you go to the man who is at death's door and say that you have not been fair towards him, that you have deprived him of his mandate under false pretences and by means of false statements? Hon. Mr. Fisher would at last have the satisfaction of knowing before he dies that 
hon. gentlemen have not been fair to him. I hope they will do so. I wpuld be putting it rather strongly to say that they robbed us; but I contend that they secured the election of Chateauguay by means of that bridge scheme which they never had any intention to carry out. It was merely a mean electoral trick on their part. I charge you, gentlemen, with having secured the votes in that constituency under false pretences and let me assure you that in our part of the country we know how to deal with men who resort to such tactics. They may change names and go under various alliases, but we know where to find them and how to inflict the punishment they deserve.
There is another thing which the Liberal party will recommend when it gets into power. I refer to the widening of the Victoria bridge where a most painful accident occurred. The bridge is too narrow for pedestrians and vehicles. Last summer there was a collision between two motor cars and the result was that a young man, 25 years of age, fell over the parapet and was drowned. It is absolutely necessary that the bridge should be widened. We have granted millions upon millions to the Victoria Bridge Company with a view to securing a good and safe throughfare. The road must be improved in order to avoid a repetition of the accident which occurred last summer. The man who caused the accident was arrested and he is to be tried in March next. I hope he will come out of it all right. But, unfortunately we had to deplore the death of a citizen of St. Constant.
A bridge must also be built at Longueuil. The necessity of such a bridge was evidenced, last summer, when the Victoria Bridge was damaged by fire. The latter remainded closed for a long time causing much inconvenience to the public. I say to the hon. member of Chambly-Verchhres (Mr. Archambault) : " You will have to make superhuman efforts, sir, to secure for your constituency the bridge which it needs so badly, and if you require my help as I need your own for the construction of a bridge between Vaudreuil and St. Anne, I shall give it to you. We shall reciprocate.
Before taking my seat, there is one question of vital importance for me that I would like to discuss.
I mean the protection we owe to the farmers, to the tobacco growers. There is in this country a considerable industry in the hands of the farmers, the tobacco industry. I have had the honour of representing the county of Montcalm for twa

sessions, and I know what takes place there.
I told these good electors in leaving that county to represent the county of Jacques-Cartier, that they would not lose me; that any aid, protection and work which your humble servant could do, should be forthcoming on behalf of those to whom I owe so much. The hon. member from Montcalm (Mr. Seguin) who succeeded me has done all that was possible for him to do, and has fulfilled his duty thoroughly. I have nothing that I could reproach him, but he has not yet succeeded in obtaining from the Government the aid and protection which we owe to these good electors. We have an important industry, that of tobacco growing. Lately there have been delagations, steps have been taken associations have been formed, to promote the interest of tobacco raising in the country, and I am sure that the Westerners, the men of Kent and Essex, the hon. members who represent these electoral districts, will not forget this industry. They will insist, I am sure, in asking that the Government do justice to these tobacco growers. What must be done, Mr. Speaker? When Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in power, when I entered this House for the first time, I began to agitate to better the condition of the tobacco growers and we succeeded very well. From a tax of ten cents a pound which existed then upon the importation of foreign tobacco, by virtue of many solicitations, of untiring insistence, of repeatedly renewing the attack, we succeeded in having the tax upon foreign tobacco fixed at 28 cents per pound. It was a great improvement that helped the electors of Montcalm, Kent, Essex, Berthier, L'As-somption, Farnham, Joliette and Terrebonne. It enabled these electors to succeed in their work, to better their social positions and the condition of their families, and, thank God, the men who laboured for the tobacco interest from 1896 to 1911 have done meritorious work. The duty on foreign tobacco should be considerably increased by the Government; I mean by the Liberal Government when it comes to power. For I have not much confidence in the present Government, I have not much confidence that it will do anything to better the condition of the planters; we must wait for the Liberals. Foreign tobacco still comes into our country in altogether too large a proportion. We still import about 20 million pounds of foreign tobacco, while in fact this importation should be kept down to a dozen million pounds at most. The
consequence would be that our growers would produce more tobacco, would improve its quality, would make greater sacrifices to make it more desirable, more marketable, and a higher duty would insure enormous profits to the planter. The rate of duty which we should ask is immaterial but it must be sufficiently high to hamper in a due measure the coming in of the foreign tobacco which is competing with our Canadian product. This, Sir, is what should be done for the growers who have done us the honour of electing us in our respective counties, and to whom it would only be doing justice.
There is an industry, Sir, which does not exist in this country, but which should. Our farmers should be given the protection necessary to encourage them to grow beets. None but the farmers understand the importance and the necessity of Go.vernment protection for this industry, which is nonexistent in Quebec. How is it that beetgrowing is a successful industry in Ontario and that we do not have it in Quebec? How can this be explained? It is because the ministers who represent us do not take the trouble to study these agricultural questions, and abandon the farmers in their difficulties. How is it that the hon. member from St. Anns (the Right Hon. Mr. Doherty) who has to represent us in the cabinet does not take the necessary measures to protect the beet industry in this country? The hon. minister will say: "That does not concern me."
The hon. Minister of Justice will say: "It is none of my business, why should I bother about beets? Is it worth my while?" If the hon. minister knew how important and necessary it is, for the farmers of the province of Quebec to establish the beet industry, he would give a premium- to farmers to encourage them to make preparations for this new industry. In doing this he would render a very great service to the electors, especially to those from the country.
The minister is bound to help us-he is appointed for that special purpose, to safeguard the interests of the people. Let me therefore tell the minister, that if he only devoted a fraction of his time to this industry, we should be very grateful to him, and when the time for his retirement comes, which by the way is near at hand, ha would have the satisfaction of saying: "When I was in office, I did something for my electors." We, therefore await with confidence his answer, trusting he will give

this matter his serious consideration, in our behalf, we, the people of the farming community'll made mention of "we" with a purpose, as I am in need of this industry at home in order to improve my farm and help to defray the expenses of the cattle that are in my stables. The beetroot industry would prove very advantageous in order to enable us to further improve our farms.	j ,	<
Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Justice to a matter which is of mutual interest to both of us. This is the request I addressed to him during the past years: Do construct a viaduct or a tunnel under the canal so that the people of the cities of Emard, C6te Saint Paul and Saint Gabriel may circulate to and fro with ease, without apprehension and loss of time between their home and Montreal. I have shown the minister in what sad plight these people are. One would imagine he was deaf. Yet he seems to be all attention when I make a request, but I must add that he very seldom gratifies my wishes. I insisted on the importance and necessity of having this tunnel built. Can you imagine a population of
15.000	to 20,000 and even more, perhaps
30.000	souls waiting patiently for boats to pass through the canal so that the bridge may be opened to traffic again and allow them_ to return to work? Yes, a hardworking class of the people, where fathers, boys and girls are to be found awaiting patiently and wondering when the bridge will open so that they may proceed to their daily work. If they arrive half an hour late, the employer who checks them will deduct so much an hour, so much a day for the lost time. To think that the honourable minister is responsible for all this! I further charge him with turning a deaf ear to all these legitimate requests of my electors. His home is there in the neighbourhood and if he does not know the facts of the case, he should go and see for himself and verify the facts. These poor people are constantly writing to me as follows: "Mr. Lafortune, for God's sake when shall we have a tunnel?" I can only answer: When it will please the Minister of Justice who is your representative, to build one-sorry to say he is not often willing."A flood occurred and a number of people barely escaped being drowned; the bridge was carried away and nc means, absolutely no means was left to cross over. This does not concern the minister for he lives in his palace, his family is free from cares, he has no anxiety,

If he only felt the pangs of anxiety, if he but knew what transpires in the life of these poor people, perhaps he would stop to think. But the honourable minister will come before the people, perhaps he will soon be seeking from these good people a renewal of their confidence. They will say to him: Sir, that tunnel that Mr. Lafortune so often begged of you, what has become of it? Where is it? It is still to be built. It is not important, no, of no importance whatever-it will open his eyes.1
These are things that the Liberal party will have to do when they return to office. All our pledges to the people between the years 1896 and 1911, such as assistance, help and protection we have fulfilled.
Mr. Speaker, I have enumerated a number of things which the Liberal party will be called to do when they ascend to power. We shall ask these gentlemen who sit across the floor of this House to render a strict account of the things they have done, those they have left undone and the good deeds they might have done. Far in the distant past these words were flashed across a wall: "Counted, weighed and found wanting." Well, we shall weigh these honourable gentlemen's actions and shall ascertain whether they come up to the mark and have fulfilled the requirements. As for myself, your humble servant, I am a Liberal and will continue to be one as long as my confidence rests with my leaders.
I am not the slave of any one; I have no need of the favours of any political party in order to live; I will remain in the ranks of the Liberal party as long as I have confidence in the leaders who are an honour to the party-
At the time of the 1911 election, in Montcalm, a young man offered himself and was selected a candidate by a substantial majority of his fellow citizens. Your humble servant refused to have his name go to the convention. I said: "No, sir, I have no time to bother with that kind of conventions. I will put my name before the great convention, before the general convention of all the electors of the county of Montcalm, and if a gentleman of the opposite party comes forward hoping to succeed through a division of the Liberal vote, I have signed my declaration and have had it published in the newspapers,
I will retire, will shake hands with the candidate chosen at the convention, and we shall crush the opponent". That is what I said in my declaration of principles, my declaration of faith. I am a Liberal, but

I do not bend my knee before men; before God, yes, but not before men. So long as I have confidence I will remain with my leader, I will remain with my party, I will remain the Liberal I am. Meanwhile, I pledge my loyalty to England, my heart to my country. Above all, I remain a faithful lover of Liberty.
On the motion of Mr. Blake, the debate was adjourned.
On the motion of Right Hon. C. J. Doherty, the House adjourned at 11.10 p.m.
Friday, February 25th, 1921
